analysis.one_liner: Rewrites federal pesticide safety rules, setting a stricter health standard for children's food and speeding approvals for new pesticides.
analysis.headline: Passed the House 417-0 and the Senate without a dissenting voice, and the President signed it into law on August 3, 1996 as Public Law 104-170.
analysis.plain_summary: This law changed how the government decides how much pesticide residue is allowed on food. It replaced the old zero-risk standard (the Delaney clause) with a 'reasonable certainty of no harm' test and required regulators to consider children's eating habits and sensitivity, adding an extra ten-fold safety margin for infants and children. It also required the EPA to re-review hundreds of older pesticide tolerances and to screen chemicals for hormone-like effects. At the same time, it gave pesticide makers favorable terms: new minor-use registration programs, longer exclusive rights to their data, faster antimicrobial approvals, and it generally blocks states from setting stricter residue limits than the federal government.
analysis.who_benefits: Everyone who eats food, especially infants and children, who get a stronger safety standard with an extra ten-fold protection margin and priority re-review of old tolerance levels [S4][S5]. Farmers growing specialty and minor crops gain a USDA minor-use program, grant funding, and faster reviews [S3][S6]. Pesticide makers gain the end of the zero-risk Delaney standard, state preemption on residue limits, extended data exclusivity, and faster antimicrobial registration [S3][S4][S6].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Food consumers, especially infants and children

how_it_helps.text: Requires that a pesticide residue tolerance only stay in effect if EPA finds a 'reasonable certainty that no harm will result from aggregate exposure,' replacing the older, weaker framework for processed foods [S4][S6].

Requires EPA to assess risks using children's food-consumption patterns, their special susceptibility, and cumulative effects, and to apply an additional ten-fold safety margin for infants and children [S4][S5].
Requires reassessment of tolerances for older pesticides during reregistration and an expedited review of tolerances already on the books [S3][S4].
Establishes a screening program for chemicals with estrogenic or other endocrine effects and requires action to protect public health if harm is found [S4].
Increases monitoring of pesticide residues in imported and domestic food and requires lay-readable pesticide residue information posted at large grocers [S2][S4].
Creates minor-use registration programs, USDA grant funding, and expedited review (within 12 months) so growers of small-acreage crops keep access to needed pesticides [S3][S6].

analysis.who_pays: Pesticide manufacturers bear new testing, data, and fee costs, and can lose registrations for chemicals that fail the new children's safety standard [S3][S4][S5]. Taxpayers fund USDA data collection, integrated pest management programs, and public health pesticide studies authorized at $12 million for fiscal 1997 [S3][S6]. Consumers, in exchange for the stronger federal standard, lose the ability of their own states to set stricter residue limits in most cases [S2][S4].
analysis.who_pays_short: Pesticide makers, taxpayers, and state regulatory authority

drawbacks.text: The law generally prohibits states from enforcing pesticide residue limits stricter than federal tolerances, and sets up petition procedures for exceptions; state-level food safety rules are largely preempted [S2][S4].

It replaces the old zero-risk Delaney clause with a risk-benefit standard that allows tolerances for residues with non-threshold (carcinogenic-type) effects if the use's benefits outweigh the risk, so some residues once banned outright can remain legal [S4].

It removes the mandatory five-year cancellation of pesticide registrations, allows continued sale of existing stocks of suspended or canceled pesticides without a finding that the use is environmentally safe, and sets a goal of reviewing registrations only every 15 years [S3][S5].

It gives registrants extended exclusive rights to their data, data waivers for minor uses, fee exemptions for public-health pesticides, and a faster, more forgiving antimicrobial registration process [S3][S5].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The public health core is real and strong: a health-based safety standard explicitly built around infants and children, an extra ten-fold margin, aggregate and cumulative exposure assessment, endocrine screening, and mandatory re-review of hundreds of old tolerances. But the same bargain gave pesticide makers significant wins — an end to the zero-risk standard, near-total preemption of stricter state limits, longer data exclusivity, and softer cancellation rules. The net effect depends heavily on how strictly EPA enforces the new standard; consumers got a better federal rule while giving up the option of tougher state ones.

outcome.mechanism: It swept the House 417-0 under a suspension-of-the-rules vote that only needed a two-thirds majority, the Senate passed it unchanged by unanimous consent the next day, and the President signed it on August 3, 1996.

narrative.text: Introduced May 12, 1995 by Rep. Tom Bliley (R-VA) and referred jointly to the Agriculture and Energy and Commerce Committees [S1][S8].
Both committees held hearings and markups over more than a year, and the bill was reported amended from Agriculture (H. Rept. 104-669 Part I) and Commerce (Part II) in July 1996 [S8].
On July 23, 1996 the House passed the bill 417-0 under suspension of the rules, with 187 of 198 Democrats, 229 of 234 Republicans, and the sole Independent voting yes [S8][S9].
The Senate passed it without amendment by unanimous consent on July 24, 1996; the President signed it on August 3, 1996, making it Public Law 104-170 [S8][S6].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Consumers gained a stronger children-focused food safety standard, and the pesticide industry simultaneously gained relief from the Delaney zero-risk rule, state preemption, and faster registration pathways.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Consumers and the pesticide industry both gained

sides.party_line_note: Support was unanimous: every voting member of both parties backed it in the House (187 of 198 Democrats, 229 of 234 Republicans), and the Senate passed it by unanimous consent.

industries.note: The law locks in pesticide makers as the sole owners of registration data with extended exclusivity for minor uses, gives them data waivers, fee exemptions, faster antimicrobial reviews, and shields them from stricter state residue limits through federal preemption [S3][S4]. At the same time they bear new testing costs and can lose registrations for chemicals that fail the stricter children's safety standard [S3][S4].

The minor-use program, USDA grant funding, and 12-month expedited reviews keep pesticides available for crops with small acreage that makers might otherwise abandon [S3][S6]. Growers are also excluded from the new civil penalty for introducing adulterated food [S4].

The law excludes liquid chemical sterilants used on medical devices from pesticide regulation, sets fast review deadlines (as short as 90 days for similar products), and exempts household antimicrobial products from certain storage and disposal rules [S3][S6].
